what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Fractal Semantic Graph names graphs of graphs of graphs
sections.para: After six months calling it "graphs of graphs of graphs", I named it Fractal Semantic Graph, defined it and published evidence. Seven live graphs, from the text of a law down to a threat in one line of code, were built with one method. This is the canonical copy of the introduction.

sections.label: Four words, and only one of them is new
sections.line: Fractal means every node opens its own world
sections.para: A graph is nodes and edges; a semantic graph gives edges verbs with named inverses; an ontology is the agreed vocabulary. Fractal adds that zooming into any node opens a new world with its own types and verbs, like a regulation into articles into terms. No top, no bottom, only altitude.

sections.label: The test is what happens at a link
sections.line: It is fractal only if a link crosses ontologies
sections.para: A risk register is a rich semantic graph but not fractal, since it stays in one vocabulary. Fractal means a link jumps worlds: from the register to security operations, to the DNS estate, to a single TCP packet. Four ontologies, one path of named edges, no adapter, because each world shares the grammar.

sections.label: Everything is already a graph, including every file format
sections.line: Every file format is already a graph, unnamed
sections.para: Regulations, PDFs, spreadsheets, codebases and JSON are already graphs; they only need named edges. Then a question crosses formats in one traversal, a superseded node shows what was built on it, the smallest node is what the question needs, each world keeps its vocabulary, and provenance reaches the byte.

sections.label: The grammar is short, and one rule does most of the work
sections.line: Five grammar rules, and relates_to is banned outright
sections.para: Each altitude has its own schema but shares five rules: verbs in both directions with real inverses, relates_to banned, properties carry data not meaning, supersede never delete, render answers not whole graphs. An edge without a verb constrains nothing, and the verb's granularity sets the precision of later questions.

sections.label: The evidence: eleven altitudes, seven vaults, one grammar
sections.line: Joining two graphs found eight amended articles neither knew
sections.para: Eleven altitudes run from law to compute instance: the EU AI Act graph has 1,523 nodes, AIUC-1 has 53 controls and 11,610 edges. Of 1,126 text crosswalks, 62 resolved, showing 8 of 27 articles had since been amended. A threat model traces one SQL injection to revenue, and GDPR Article 45 shows meaning flipping.

sections.label: What is still modelled rather than imported
sections.line: Several altitudes are still modelled; gaps are named
sections.para: The threat model's bottom four altitudes are authored, not imported from a CMDB or cloud account. No graph yet joins enterprise architecture to obligations. Crosswalks resolve only at article level, six of the GDPR atlas's 227 edges use the banned verb, and the agent altitude has 23 primitives but no real permission import.

sections.label: Why now
sections.line: Cheap edge naming, acting agents and lost schema wars
sections.para: Three changes make it practical: a language model now proposes verbs faster than humans type, so the bottleneck is purpose. Agents act on the world, so claims must trace to their source byte. And nobody won the schema wars, so the only surviving model lets everyone connect without conforming.

sections.label: Open them
sections.line: Every graph is live with published read-only keys
sections.para: All the graphs can be opened, with read keys published on purpose that cannot write, walking down from the law or up from compute. Links go to sgit.ai/demos/fractal-graphs, the VoiceDebrief vault, graphs.sgit.ai and its llms.txt grammar, standards.sgit.ai and abp.sgit.ai. The article is licensed CC BY 4.0.
